prompt: What does `volatile` on `stop` forbid the compiler to do?
hint: The freedom that broke lesson 12's program.

choices.text: Run the worker on a different processor from `main`
choices.why: Scheduling is untouched.

choices.text: Compile the loop at all
choices.why: The loop was compiled, and ran 3.7 billion times.

choices.text: Read the field once and keep it
choices.why: Right: every read goes to memory.

choices.text: Write the field from more than one thread at a time
choices.why: Any thread may still write it.

prompt: The `volatile` loop spun about 3.7 billion times in a second. What does that say about the cost of a `volatile` read on x86?

choices.text: Little more than a plain read
choices.why: Right: x86 already keeps reads in order.

choices.text: It costs nothing, because the JIT removes it
choices.why: The JIT may not remove it; that is the point.

choices.text: It costs as much as a lock taken on every turn of the loop
choices.why: Nothing in the run suggests that.

choices.text: It is expensive, and the loop would be faster without it
choices.why: Without it the loop never ended at all.

prompt: Which two promises does `volatile` make? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Writes before it are visible after a read that sees it
choices.why: Yes: ordering.

choices.text: A read sees the latest write to the field
choices.why: Yes: visibility.

choices.text: `count++` on it runs as one step
choices.why: No: section 04.

choices.text: Only one thread may write it
choices.why: No such restriction.

prompt: In `Handoff.java`, `ready = true` is moved above `copies = 3`. What may the consumer now print?
hint: Which writes does the promise cover?

choices.text: The same line, every time
choices.why: It may; nothing guarantees it any more.

choices.text: Nothing: it compiles but never starts
choices.why: The consumer still sees `ready` and prints.

choices.text: A compile error about the order
choices.why: The compiler checks nothing here.

choices.text: `0 copies`
choices.why: Right: that write is no longer before the flag.

prompt: Inside a busy-wait loop, `Thread.___()` tells the processor the thread is spinning.
Four threads did `count++` a million times each on a `volatile long`. Why was the total short?

choices.text: Both read one value, both wrote it plus one
choices.why: Right: a lost update.

choices.text: `volatile` writes are sometimes dropped
choices.why: Every write happened; some overwrote others.

choices.text: Some threads ended before the others started
choices.why: That would give the right total.

choices.text: A `long` is too small for four million
choices.why: It holds far more.

prompt: Match each tool with what it does about `count++`.

pairs.right: makes each read and write visible, and nothing more
lets one thread at a time run the three steps
does the three steps as one operation

right_distractors: runs the three steps on three processors

prompt: Reading a value, changing it and writing it back is a ___-modify-write.
hint: The first of the three steps.

prompt: Which field is a good fit for `volatile`?
hint: Each write independent of the current value.

choices.text: A shutdown flag set by one thread
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: A minimum and a maximum that must agree
choices.why: They are visible one at a time, never as a pair.

choices.text: A count of requests
choices.why: Same problem as `count++`.

choices.text: A running total of sales
choices.why: The new total depends on the old.

prompt: In `Lazy.java`, what would go wrong if `index` were not `volatile`?
hint: The fast path takes no lock.

choices.text: The index would be built twice, once by each thread
choices.why: The second check, inside the lock, prevents that.

choices.text: `synchronized` would stop working
choices.why: It works; the fast path does not use it.

choices.text: The program would not compile without the keyword
choices.why: It compiles either way.

choices.text: A fast-path thread could see it unfinished
choices.why: Right: unsafe publication.

prompt: Before writing double-checked locking, what does the lesson suggest considering?

choices.text: Calling `System.gc()` first
choices.why: Irrelevant.

choices.text: A nested holder class, or eager building
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: A parallel stream to build it on every processor
choices.why: Irrelevant to initialising once.

choices.text: Making every field in the class `volatile` as well
choices.why: That does not make the build happen once.

prompt: Put the lost update of the figure in order.
A price list is shared as `static volatile List<Long> prices`, and an admin thread calls `prices.add(...)` on it. Is that safe?
hint: What is volatile: the field, or the list?

choices.text: Yes, if the admin thread is the only writer
choices.why: Readers may still see the list mid-change.

choices.text: No, because `List<Long>` cannot be volatile
choices.why: Any field can be volatile.

choices.text: Yes: `volatile` covers the list's contents
choices.why: It covers the field, the reference.

choices.text: No: only the reference is volatile
choices.why: Right: replace a whole immutable list instead, lesson 12's `PriceList` pattern.
